The agent probed the infrastructure, went away for 11 hours, then came back with an exploit.  Timing how long the exploit code took to run is absolutely ridiculous.  To make an analogy: it's like someone writing an essay, timing how long it took them to physically hand it in to the professor, then saying "completing the essay took 1.3 seconds".  While technically correct (the essay was not completed until it was handed in). Any reasonable person is going to thinking "completing an essay" means from start to finish.  AI can do some tasks very fast. But these types of metrics are intentionally misleading. They're designed to spread FUD and delude people about how fast AI attacks actually are.  ARTEX did not hack the admin account in 1.3 seconds. ARTEX spend 11 hours developing attack tools and one of the tools took 1.3 seconds to run (that's actually fairly slow for code, but not unreasonable).  The point of focus should be that the AI was able to weaponize a vulnerability in 11 hours (it would likely take a human much longer), not that the exploit took 1.3 second to run (it would take a human the exact same amount of time).

When you delete something, it doesn't get erased, the space is just marked as unused. The actual data stay put until the space is needed for something else, at which point it gets overwritten.  It's very annoying because I can still see exactly which website was responsible for the malware infection, because that data is still there, but because the database record was unlinked, all the metadata is gone.  So I can't offer a  nice neat "X led to Y which led to Z" type explanation. I just have to be like "well these two things happened, and that implies that maybe this other thing happened, but correlation does not equal causation"😭

You can tell who doesn't work in cybersecurity, because they're convinced it's a great time to be in the industry because "more cyberattacks means more cybersecurity spending".  It's a great time to be a shareholder, and that's about it.   I am not aware of a single company that operates on the basis of "cyberattacks are up 10%, we need to hire 10% more defenders".  What actually happens, is 10% more cyberattacks means 10% more work for the same pay. And the workload just keeps increasing until people end up burning out and quitting, or worse.  At some point if things get bad enough, a company may, and that is a very heavy lifting "may", find budget for additional headcount.  But, like, go find me someone who works in cyber defense and isn't burnt out, and I'll find you someone who doesn't do any work.  Cybersecurity is one of those industries where IMO the salaries only look good on paper.   If you're coming from a minimum wage customer service job, it's definitely a huge improvement. But if you're going into white collar work anyway, there's so many jobs that pay well and won't burn you out.
